15-1.title: Reading Your Waits
15-1.subtitle: Name the tiles that would finish the hand

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Time to read a hand like a map. Thirteen tiles, one tile away from winning.

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: The tiles that would finish it are called your waits. Every wait has a name.

dialogues.speaker: you
dialogues.text: So I just look at the shape and work out what fits?

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Exactly. Four melds and a pair. Find the hole, name the wait.

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Get these automatic and you will see waits in your sleep.

questions.question: This hand has three complete melds, one pair, and a partly built meld waiting for its last tile. How many different tiles would finish it? {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s5}}{{east}}{{east}}
questions.explanation: You are waiting on m1, m4 and m7 — three different tiles, all of them one step from a meld.

questions.question: Which of these tiles would finish the hand below? {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s5}}{{east}}{{east}}
questions.explanation: m1 makes 123, m4 makes 234 with the m2 m3 already there, and m7 makes 567 with m5 m6. p8 completes nothing.

questions.question: You hold {{p8}}{{p9}} at the end of this hand. Which single tile would finish it? {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{east}}{{east}}{{p8}}{{p9}}
questions.explanation: Only p7 turns p8 p9 into 789. This is called an edge wait 邊張 because it sits at the end of the suit.

questions.question: The hand below is waiting on {{p8}} with {{p7}} and {{p9}} in hand. What is this wait called? {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{east}}{{east}}{{p7}}{{p9}}
questions.explanation: A tile sitting between two others, filling the gap, is a closed wait 坎張 — here p7 p9 waiting for p8.

questions.question: Look again at the hand waiting on {{p7}} with {{p8}}{{p9}}. Why is it called an edge wait 邊張 rather than a closed wait?
options: Because the wait sits on the last possible tile of the suit
Because the winning tile is an honour
Because the pair is used as the eyes
Because two different tiles would finish it
questions.explanation: p8 p9 can only be finished by p7, at the very edge of the suit — a closed wait has a gap with tiles on both sides.

questions.question: Match each wait to how it looks.

pairs.right: e.g. {{p5}}{{p6}} waiting on p4 or p7
One tile left, waiting to pair it

questions.explanation: The four shapes cover almost every wait you will ever hold: two-sided, edge, closed and single.

questions.question: This hand is waiting on a single tile as its pair. How many copies of that tile can still be in play? {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{red}}
questions.explanation: You hold one red yourself, so the other three are still somewhere in the wall or in other hands.

questions.question: This is the thirteen orphans hand, one tile short. Which statements are true? {{m1}}{{m9}}{{p1}}{{p9}}{{s1}}{{s9}}{{east}}{{south}}{{west}}{{north}}{{red}}{{green}}{{white}}
options: It waits on all thirteen orphan types
It waits on one specific tile only
Three copies of each winning tile are still live
Any of those tiles can finish it
questions.explanation: Thirteen orphans waits on all thirteen ones, nines and honours; you already hold one of each, so three copies of every winning tile remain.

15-2.title: Counting Outs
15-2.subtitle: How many tiles can actually save you

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: A wait is worth nothing if every copy is already gone. Now we count.

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Four of each tile exist. Subtract what you hold and what everyone has shown.

dialogues.speaker: you
dialogues.text: So a wide wait can still be a dead wait?

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Exactly. Outs is the honest number, not the shape on paper.

dialogues.speaker: mj
dialogues.text: Count outs before you count faan. It changes what you throw.

questions.question: This hand is waiting on m1, m4 and m7. Counting every copy still in play, how many outs does it have? {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s5}}{{east}}{{east}}
questions.explanation: Four m1, three m4 (you hold one) and four m7 make eleven live outs.

questions.question: Same hand, but two m4 and one m1 have already been discarded and are visible. How many outs are left? {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{p5}}{{p6}}{{p7}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{s5}}{{east}}{{east}}
questions.explanation: Eleven minus three visible copies leaves eight; the shape did not change, only the supply did.

questions.question: This hand is waiting on p1 or p4. How many live copies does it have in total? {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{m7}}{{m8}}{{m9}}{{p1}}{{p2}}{{p3}}{{p4}}
questions.explanation: You hold one p1 and one p4, so three of each remain: six outs.

questions.question: Match each hand to its number of live outs.

pairs.left: Seven pairs, holding six pairs and a single

questions.explanation: Nine gates waits on nine tiles, thirteen orphans on thirteen, one pair wait on three, and the mixed hand on eleven.

questions.question: Which statements about outs are true?
options: Outs are the live copies of every tile that would finish your hand
A two-sided wait always has more outs than two single waits
Copies you hold yourself reduce the outs of that tile
questions.explanation: Outs are live copies only. A two-sided wait is not automatically better than two separate single waits — you have to count.

questions.question: Hand one waits on two tiles with four copies each. Hand two waits on a single tile with three copies left. Which is the better wait?
options: Hand two, because a single wait is cleaner
questions.explanation: Eight outs against three: the wider wait is roughly twice as likely to arrive, and nothing about the shape makes the single wait better.

questions.question: This nine gates hand waits on every tile of the same suit. How many live copies does that come to? {{m1}}{{m1}}{{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{m7}}{{m8}}{{m9}}{{m9}}{{m9}}
questions.explanation: Nine waits, with one of every tile already in hand: 9 x 4 minus the six duplicate copies you hold leaves 23.

questions.question: You hold {{p7}}{{p9}} and nothing else is showing on the table. Which tile, when it appears, completes your hand? {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}}{{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}}{{east}}{{east}}{{p7}}{{p9}}
questions.explanation: p8 fills the gap between p7 and p9 — four copies are live, so it is four outs.
